Triggers.value: A specific texture associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
try hard not think about the trauma
I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

vignette:
It happened on Black Friday. Marcus was thirty-three then, working the electronics aisle at a big-box store, helping a customer with a television when the crowd at the front entrance surged. He never saw what started it—someone later said a woman had fainted, another said a fight over a discounted tablet—but he felt the pressure of bodies pressing forward, the heat and the panic, and then the sound of a child screaming. He was pinned against a display for nearly four minutes, his cheek pressed against the cold metal shelving, and what he remembers most is not the pain but the texture of the carpet beneath his fingers—rough, industrial, slightly greasy—as he tried to brace himself. A man beside him was yelling at people to stop pushing, and Marcus watched that man’s face twist with rage and fear, and he felt something collapse inside him. He was not badly hurt physically, but when he finally got free, he walked out of the store and drove home in silence, and he has not been able to think about that day without his stomach clenching ever since.

Three years later, Marcus works at a smaller hardware store, but even there the triggers find him. Crowds are the worst—whenever more than a few customers cluster near the register, his throat tightens and his palms go damp. But it is not just crowds. He has come to believe that certain people are dangerous, that the way they carry themselves or the tone of their voice signals a willingness to push, to trample, to do whatever it takes to get what they want. He watches shoppers closely now, scanning for the ones who seem impatient or entitled, and when he sees a man shove past someone to grab the last bag of mulch, Marcus feels a hot surge of shame that he cannot explain. The worst trigger, though, is the texture of his own work gloves—the rough, industrial fabric reminds him of that carpet, and he has started wearing thin cotton gloves under them, even though his manager has commented on it.

What frightens Marcus most is how real his memories feel. When he is triggered—by a crowd, by a rude customer, by the brush of his glove—the event comes back not as a story he tells himself but as a series of snapshots: the child’s face, the man’s twisted expression, the feel of the carpet. These moments are more vivid than anything happening around him, and afterwards he has to remind himself that he is not still there. He has tried to stop thinking about it altogether. He tells himself it was not that bad, that he is overreacting, that maybe it did not even happen the way he remembers. But the more he pushes the memory away, the more it seems to ambush him. Last month, a customer brushed past him in the aisle, and the sudden contact sent him straight into that spiral of images, and he had to lock himself in the stockroom for twenty minutes.

He has started hurting himself to escape. At first it was just pinching the inside of his arm when the memories got too loud, but now he sometimes scratches his forearm with the edge of a box cutter when he is alone in the back room, and the sharp sting pulls him back to the present. He knows this is not normal, but he is certain that if he stops, the memories will swallow him. His wife has noticed the scratches, and last week she asked him to talk to someone. That is what brought him here—not the shame, not the fear, but the look on her face when she saw his arm. He is afraid that if he tells the whole story, it will become even more real, and he is not sure he can survive that.
